read.sections.0.heading.source: Your feed is chosen for you
read.sections.0.heading.back: Your feed is chosen for you

read.sections.0.text.source: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you watched, liked or skipped before, and guesses what you will want to see. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people if they were happy with what they saw. A feed can be useful. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena's feed found her a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed showed him mostly posts about the new sports field.
read.sections.0.text.back: People post far more than anyone can see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes into your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you have watched, liked or skipped, and guesses what you want to see. Each app has different aims. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people whether they were satisfied with what they saw. A feed can be useful. In Maplebrook, a made-up town, Lena's feed found her a free video lesson about writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed mostly showed posts about the new sports field.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Feed" is "suapan" (DBP; shared TERMS.md). Malaysian young people often say "feed" in English; a reviewer should check "suapan" is understood.

Ravi's feed showed him posts about the new sports field.

Ravi's feed showed posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A rumour can spread faster than the truth
read.sections.1.heading.back: A rumour can spread faster than the truth

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of Twitter. They looked at about 126,000 news stories shared from 2006 to 2017, each checked by fact-checking groups. On Twitter in those years, false stories spread further and faster than true ones. They were often more surprising, and people shared them, not only robot accounts. The study looked at what people chose to share on one site, not at how feeds pick posts. This matters before an election, when people need correct facts to vote. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote had moved to Friday. It was shared 900 times in one day, and the correct notice only 60 times.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study about Twitter. They looked at about 126,000 news stories shared from 2006 to 2017, each one checked by fact-checking groups. On Twitter in those years, false news spread further and faster than true news. False news was often more surprising, and it was humans who shared it, not only robot accounts. The study looked at what people chose to share on one site, not how feeds choose posts. This matters before an election, when people need correct facts to vote. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote had been moved to Friday. That rumour was shared 900 times in one day, and the correct notice only 60 times.

read.sections.2.text.source: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. Ravi saw mostly posts for the sports field, and Lena saw mostly posts for the library. But a review of many studies found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. Since 2024, a European Union law has said that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. They must also offer a feed that isn't based on what they know about you. You can help too: follow different sources, and check before you share.
read.sections.2.text.back: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. Ravi mostly saw posts supporting the sports field, and Lena mostly saw posts supporting the library. But a review of many studies found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people assume. Since 2024, a European Union law has set out that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. The apps must also offer a feed that is not based on what they know about you. You can help too: follow different sources, and check before you share.

watch.summary.source: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show you posts that will keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. Experts in the video say this isn't always a good thing. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full view of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.
watch.summary.back: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. In many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you do not see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone has built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show posts that will keep you interested, so that you keep scrolling. Experts in this video say this is not always good. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full picture of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.

educatorNotes.0.source: The research in section 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018): about 126,000 cascades of news stories on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap held with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories that fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not all posts). It measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need separate study.
educatorNotes.0.back: The research in passage 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018): about 126,000 sharing cascades of news on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true news took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap remained even with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories investigated by fact-checkers (contested stories, not all posts). The study measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need to be studied separately.

educatorNotes.1.source: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review found echo chambers much less widespread than commonly assumed and no support for the filter bubble idea. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying in full from 17 February 2024, and earlier to very large platforms (over 45 million monthly users in the EU), four months after the Commission designated them; they must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.
educatorNotes.1.back: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; do not reduce them to one motive only. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review found echo chambers far less widespread than commonly assumed and no support for the filter bubble idea. That European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying fully from 17 February 2024, and earlier for very large platforms (over 45 million users a month in the EU), four months after the Commission designated their status; those platforms must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one system not based on profiling, and assess risks such as election manipulation.
